corrections.stars_or_usage: 38 stars, 11 forks; AMD's official AOCL component (commits titled 'Updates for AOCL 5.0 Release' through 'Updates for AOCL 5.3.2 Release'; the GitHub Releases section is empty)
corrections.caveats: Tier D: no published numbers in the README, tools/benchmark/benchmark_guide.md or docs/User_Guide.md; amd.com was unreachable here (DNS failure) and a web search found no AMD-published percentage. The benchmark tool (bench.py, default '-perf d' Glibc vs LibMem report) makes the claim checkable on Zen hardware. Default build uses page-boundary-safe unmasked over-reads for small sizes (ALMEM_STRICT_BOUNDS=Y gives a masked strict-bounds variant); an AVX-512 build crashes on non-AVX-512 CPUs; IFUNC needs recent toolchains; binaries built against glibc 2.34+ need glibc 2.34+ at run time. notes: Accurate record; tier D because AMD publishes no numbers in the repo. Keep as AMD's official Zen-tuned libc string/memory replacement (notable despite 38 stars); shortcoming: no published measurements, claims must be reproduced with the shipped bench.py on Zen hardware.

tier_reason: README tables compare hand-written SSE assembly (bzero6.S, bzero7.S) against libc memset (bzero_0 in bzero.c) using the public harness main.c on named CPUs (Xeon E5520, i7-4850HQ), and every number in claimed_speedup matches. Not A: the build flags for the published 2017 runs are not stated (the 2017 Makefile at e807b1d sets no CFLAGS, i.e. gcc's default -O0; the current Makefile adds only -march=native; the README merely says only 'gcc -O2' works as expected), and the gcc and glibc versions are not given.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated). Published flags unclear: the 2017 Makefile (commit e807b1d) sets only CC=gcc with no CFLAGS (gcc default -O0); the current Makefile sets CFLAGS=-march=native with no -O level; the README says only 'gcc -O2' gives naive C results and that clang -O2 or gcc -O3 may rewrite the C versions into memset. The assembly versions do not depend on the -O level.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Core i7-4850HQ (total microseconds for 10,000 calls): 32 B bzero_6 26 / bzero_7 23 vs memset 86 (3.3x / 3.7x, derived from page data); 64 B 26 vs 70 (2.7x, derived from page data); 256 B 51 vs 82 (1.6x, derived from page data); 1024 B 189 vs 149 and 2048 B 393 vs 241 (memset faster). Xeon E5520 (no AVX): 64 B 47 vs 71, 256 B 79 vs 127, 1024 B 265 vs 317, 2048 B bzero_6 655 / bzero_7 552 vs memset 664. The README Update says newer AVX versions (bzero_9..bzero_H, added 2019) are 'faster than memset() for any memory size', but no tables or numbers are given for them.
corrections.caveats: Units derived from main.c: each figure is the total gettimeofday time in microseconds for 10,000 calls on the same buffer (so 23 vs 26 is within 1 us timer noise; about 2.3-2.6 ns per call); one run per size, hot cache, same size every call (branch-friendly). Published tables come from the 2017 harness (the current main.c prints a different size list) on 2009/2013 CPUs with an unstated glibc; author notes stock memset is 'sometimes unreasonably bad for small buffer sizes' there, which modern glibc ERMS/AVX2/EVEX memset paths likely fixed. Memset wins at 1024 B and 2048 B on the AVX laptop. The 2019 AVX versions have no published numbers; AVX-512 untested. Unlicense (public-domain dedication, no patent grant).

notes: Numbers verified exactly; downgraded A to C because the flags and compiler/glibc versions behind the 2017 tables are not stated (2017 Makefile builds at gcc default -O0 while the README implies -O2). Shortcomings: tiny single-run microsecond totals, old CPUs and glibc, memset faster at 1 KiB and up on AVX, newest AVX variants unmeasured; 1 star.

tier_reason: First-party README table (gcc 4.9, 'msvc 2012 got a similar result') from the public harness FastMemcpy.c with stated build commands (gcc -O3 -msse2), but no CPU model and no libc version, so C; all quoted numbers match the README.

corrections.caveats: Implementation is SSE2/AVX intrinsics (85 _mm_ calls in FastMemcpy.h, 91 in FastMemcpy_Avx.h, no inline asm), so it is a memcpy-baseline entry rather than hand-written assembly. CPU model and glibc version not stated; the README results are from 2015 (gcc 4.9 / MSVC 2012); the 2017 AVX version has no published numbers. Only one README row is slower (1 MiB, both aligned: 181 vs 165 ms); the others show gains. Harness flaws (FastMemcpy.c): same src/dst and size every call (hot cache, perfectly predicted branches), millisecond gettimeofday timer, memcpy always runs first on freshly malloc'd buffers, benchmark() not marked noinline so sizes may be constant-propagated; alexey-milovidov (issue #6) called the benchmark 'nonsense' for these reasons and saw glibc slightly faster in a ClickHouse perf test. Independent runs on newer toolchains show it slower than glibc memcpy: issue #4 (gcc 7.5.0, glibc 2.27: 32 B 230 vs 63 ms, random 1953 vs 635 ms; gcc 5.4: 512 B 77 vs 56 ms) and issue #6 (gcc 10.2.1, Clear Linux: 32 B 48 vs 35 ms, 1024 B 85 vs 41 ms, random 802 vs 662 ms). Issue #5 (gcc 4.4.7, 278 vs 85 ms at 32 B) was a build-flag mistake per the reporter.

notes: README numbers accurate, tier C stays (no CPU model). Record the shortcoming that it is not faster on modern toolchains: independent runs in issues #4 (gcc 7.5/glibc 2.27) and #6 (gcc 10.2.1) show glibc memcpy faster at most sizes and on random access, and a ClickHouse maintainer criticised the benchmark (same-size loops, possible constant propagation, no CPU details).
